title: Home Corner
strapline: Cooking the dinner, phoning nanny, tucking the baby in — the safest place to try out being a grown-up.
intent: Children replay the routines they know best — cooking, washing up, bedtime, visitors at the door — and make sense of home life by living it again on their own terms.
Family roles (mum, dad, big sister, grandad, the baby) give children a script to step into, so talk flows further than it does anywhere else in the room.
Real domestic jobs — pouring, stirring, spreading, folding, laying the table — build hand control with a genuine purpose.
Sharing one small home means constant negotiation: who sleeps in the bed, whose turn with the teapot, who answers the phone.
Children meet the idea that every family does home differently — different foods, different words, different bedtime songs — and that different is interesting.
implementation: Be a visitor, not a director: knock on the door, accept the cup of tea, ask what's for dinner — and let the children run the household.
Model the domestic talk children may not yet own: 'I'll just pop the kettle on', 'dinner's nearly ready', 'shall I wash while you dry?'
Keep resources real and open-ended — proper pans, wooden spoons, real (empty) packets from families' own kitchens, fabric for anything.
Notice the maths hiding in the housework: laying one plate per person, sharing out the pretend peas, 'have we got enough cups for everyone?'
Reflect every child's home: photos of their families, dolls with a range of skin tones, cooking pots and utensils from different food cultures.
When squabbles flare over the one frying pan, coach the negotiation rather than solving it — 'ask her when it's your turn'.
Stay long enough to sustain the story: a five-minute storyline can become a twenty-minute one with an adult gently feeding in 'oh no — the baby's woken up!'
key_questions: What's cooking? It smells delicious — who's it for?
The baby won't stop crying — what do you think she needs?
Who lives in this house? Who's coming to visit today?
Have we got enough plates for everyone at the table?
What do you do at bedtime in your house?

impact.text: Younger children replay familiar routines with real-looking props — stirring the pot, feeding teddy, phoning nanny.
Older children sustain shared family storylines, assigning and swapping roles and negotiating who has the pram.
Children narrate and direct the play aloud — 'you be the daddy, the dinner's hot, careful!'
Children pour 'tea' without spilling, spread pretend butter and handle kitchen tools with growing control.
Children lay one plate, one cup and one spoon per person, and check whether there are enough for everyone.
Children talk about their own family's ways of doing things and notice that friends' homes are different — and interesting.
Children show tenderness in role — tucking the baby in, fetching a blanket for a poorly teddy, making a visitor welcome.

enhancements: Real (clean, empty) food packets donated by families — including packets from home cuisines and with different scripts on the labels.
A washing line, pegs and doll-sized clothes for a washing day.
A real telephone or old mobile and a homemade phone book of family names.
Birthday tea provocation: candles, cards, wrapping paper and a party guest list to write.
A new baby arrives: a Moses basket, tiny clothes and a bottle appear overnight.
Recipe cards with photos so children can 'cook' a dish step by step.
Herbs, real vegetables or dried pasta in the pans for genuine sensory cooking.

playing_exploring: Children step into roles they've watched all their lives and try them on for size.
Familiar props invite children to initiate their own domestic dramas without adult prompting.
active_learning: Children persist with self-set jobs — the table must be laid, the baby must be settled — because the purpose is theirs.
creating_thinking: A pan becomes a drum, a scarf becomes a baby sling — children make one thing stand for another and build storylines of their own.
